To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the notion of “quality” is a powerful tool for the retailer–distributors in Canada to shape the direction and development of the food and wine clusters.

the quality of food and wine is contested by the various stakeholders in the food and wine cluster, and that the retailers and distributors play an important role in shaping the future quality of the cluster.
the retailer–distributer has an important influence on the development and direction of food and/or wine quality in a given cluster.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of public policy in supporting and shaping the direction of a particular food and wine cluster in Canada.
how the notion of quality is used to shape the future direction of a food–wine cluster.
the following questions: What is the role of the retailer-distributor in shaping the direction of the food and wine cluster in Canada?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“quality”-claiming clusters are not a panacea for the food and wine system, but they do offer some hope for the future.

the “quality” of a food and beverage cluster is not only determined by the quality of the product itself, but is also a function of the quality of the social relations that surround the production and consumption process.
the future of the Canadian food and wine cluster is still very much up for grabs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the future of the quality of food and wine in Canada is inextricably tied to the future of its food and wine supply chains, and the future of its supply chains will be shaped by the future direction of food and retail policy.

the future of quality-based food and wine clusters depends on the ability of policymakers to recognize and regulate the public good of quality in a manner that is not dominated by the larger retail-distributors.
we are trying to understand the social, cultural and economic dynamics of the food and wine system in Canada and how it can be improved.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the future of food and wine quality in Canada is not only dependent on the quality-claiming practices of the retailer-distributor, but also on the ability of policymakers to support and nurture the growth of localized quality-based food and wine clusters.
the future of food and wine in Canada is not only about “alternative” agro-food systems.
the “quality” of the food and wine cluster is shaped by the retailer-distributor and that this is not likely to change any time soon.
